title: Transport Systems in Mammals

standard_code: SSS 2 Biology: Transport Systems in Mammals
standard_text: The circulatory system: the structure and functions of the heart; the cardiac cycle; blood vessels (arteries, veins and capillaries); double circulation (pulmonary and systemic); blood and its components; the lymphatic system; cardiovascular diseases. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 2; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 2 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): the heart and blood vessels, the circulatory system, blood and its cells, the heart and its conduction and blood and health. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
body_html:
How to think about it

The heart has four chambers: two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out. Valves stop blood from flowing backwards. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation); the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body (systemic circulation).

Arteries have thick, elastic walls to carry blood at high pressure; veins have valves and carry blood back to the heart; capillaries have walls one cell thick for exchange. Blood is made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

Example

Which chamber pumps blood to the body?

It has the thickest wall.

Answer: the left ventricle

Example

Why do veins have valves?

Blood pressure is low.

Answer: to stop blood flowing backwards

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all arteries carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery does not).
  • Thinking the heart's left side is on your right when you look at a diagram.
  • Mixing up atria and ventricles.

faq.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker?
faq.a: It must pump blood all round the body, which needs more pressure.

faq.q: How can you reduce the risk of heart disease?
faq.a: Exercise, do not smoke, and eat less salt and saturated fat.

items.q: Stroke volume is 120 mL and heart rate is 70 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 8,400 mL min⁻¹ = 8.40 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Does the pulmonary artery carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

items.q: Which sound of the heart is 'lub'?
c: the closing of the tricuspid and bicuspid (AV) valves
the closing of the semilunar valves
items.e: 'Dub' is the closing of the semilunar valves.

items.q: Does the hepatic portal vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The hepatic portal vein carries deoxygenated blood from the small intestine to the liver.

items.q: Stroke volume is 65 cm³ and heart rate is 70 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in dm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 4,550 cm³ min⁻¹ = 4.55 dm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is the normal blood pressure of a healthy adult?
items.e: Systolic over diastolic.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the body to the right atrium?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Does the pulmonary vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

items.q: What is lymph?
c: tissue fluid in lymph vessels, containing lymphocytes
items.e: It returns fluid to the blood.

items.q: Pulmonary ventilation is 9.90 L min⁻¹ at 18 breaths per minute. Calculate the tidal volume.
items.e: Tidal volume = ventilation ÷ breathing rate = 0.550 L.

items.q: One cardiac cycle on an ECG lasts 0.80 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.e: Heart rate = 60 ÷ 0.80 = 75.0 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: What is the role of AV node?
c: passing the impulse from the atria to the ventricles
the pacemaker that starts each heartbeat
items.e: AV node: passing the impulse from the atria to the ventricles.

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for becoming macrophages that engulf germs?
items.e: Monocytes: becoming macrophages that engulf germs.

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for B and T cells of the immune response?
items.e: Lymphocytes: B and T cells of the immune response.

items.q: Stroke volume is 90 mL and heart rate is 100 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 9,000 mL min⁻¹ = 9.00 L min⁻¹.

items.q: What is the stroke volume of a healthy adult heart?
items.e: Cardiac output = 72 × 70 mL ≈ 5 L per minute.

items.q: Pulmonary ventilation is 40.0 L min⁻¹ at 20 breaths per minute. Calculate the tidal volume.
items.e: Tidal volume = ventilation ÷ breathing rate = 2.00 L.

items.q: Cardiac output is 6.00 dm³ min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 100 cm³. Calculate the heart rate.
items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 6,000 ÷ 100 = 60 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: One cardiac cycle on an ECG lasts 1.2 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.e: Heart rate = 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50.0 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: Cardiac output is 9.90 dm³ min⁻¹ and heart rate is 90 beats per minute. Calculate the stroke volume in cm³.
items.e: SV = CO ÷ HR = 9,900 cm³ ÷ 90 = 110 cm³.

items.q: Blood is in the left atrium. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Blood enters the vena cava. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Blood is in the lungs. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 75 × 60 = 4,500 cm³/min.

items.q: Blood enters the lungs. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the small intestine to the liver?

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells?

items.q: Blood enters the right ventricle. Where has it just come from?

It carries blood away from the heart.
It carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: What is angina pectoris?
c: acute chest pain when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle
items.e: It is a warning sign of heart disease.

items.q: What does the P-wave of an ECG show?
items.e: QRS shows ventricular depolarisation; T shows ventricular repolarisation.

items.q: What is the role of platelets?
c: the most abundant white blood cells (60–65%), phagocytic
the pacemaker that starts each heartbeat
releasing factors that help blood clot
passing the impulse from the atria to the ventricles
items.e: Platelets: releasing factors that help blood clot.

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for resisting infections and allergic reactions?
items.e: Eosinophils: resisting infections and allergic reactions.

items.q: Which blood group is the universal donor?
items.e: Its cells carry no A or B antigen.

items.e: AV node: passing the impulse from the atria to the ventricles.

items.q: What is the role of bundle of His?

items.e: Bundle of His: carrying the impulse down the interventricular septum.

items.e: Basophils: secreting histamine, serotonin and heparin.

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for carrying the impulse down the interventricular septum?

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for the most abundant white blood cells (60–65%), phagocytic?
items.e: Neutrophils: the most abundant white blood cells (60–65%), phagocytic.

items.q: Which condition can occur when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby for the second time?
items.e: Her anti-Rh antibodies destroy the baby's red cells.

items.q: Which is the hepatic portal system?
c: veins that carry blood from the intestine to the liver before it returns to the heart
items.e: The liver processes absorbed food.

items.q: What is the role of lymphocytes?

items.q: Why does smoking increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
c: Fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries.
Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.
items.e: In coronary heart disease, the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

items.q: Which substance in cigarette smoke: it is addictive and raises heart rate and blood pressure.
